**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.

Doshi's work on the reunification of Indian and English heritages through his practice was awarded a Global Award for Sustainable Architecture in 2007, the award's first edition. The award recognized Doshi's significant step in the direction of an alternative development model.[22]

**Anne Lacaton** (born 2 August 1955)[2] is a French architect and educator. She runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Jean-Philippe Vassal. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

She was born in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière on 2 August 1955.[2] Lacaton graduated in architecture from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux and received a master's degree in urban planning from the University of Bordeaux in 1984.[4][5] Lacaton often visited Vassal in Niger, who worked there as an architect and town planner; they built their first joint project, a straw hut.[6]

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.

Doshi's work on the reunification of Indian and English heritages through his practice was awarded a Global Award for Sustainable Architecture in 2007, the award's first edition. The award recognized Doshi's significant step in the direction of an alternative development model.[22]


In March 2018, Doshi was awarded the Pritzker Architecture Prize, the Nobel equivalent for the field, thus becoming the first Indian to receive the honour. The Pritzker jury announced that Doshi "has always created an architecture that is serious, never flashy or a follower of trends", and noted his "deep sense of responsibility and a desire to contribute to his country and its people through high quality, authentic architecture".[5]

<title>RCR Arquitectes</title>
<content>
![](image)Public Library in Barcelona, designed by RCR
**RCR Arquitectes** is a Spanish architecture firm consisting of principles and co-founders Rafael Aranda, Carme Pigem and Ramon Vilalta.[1] The trio were the 2017 recipients of the Pritzker Prize for Architecture.[2] While the firm had won many awards before the Pritzker, they were relatively unknown compared to other finalists.[2]




## History

[edit]

The firm was founded in Olot, Spain in 1988.[2]



## Style

[edit]

The firm is known for its frequent use of weathering steel in its projects.[2][*example needed*]



## Selected projects

[edit]

The firm designed the imposing Musée Soulages [fr] in Rodez, France, after winning a 2007 competition.[3]



* De Krook, the central public library and media center in Ghent, Belgium, designed in collaboration with local firm Coussée & Goris and opened in 2017.
* Celler Peralada, the first winery in Europe to receive the golden LEED certificate for Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design.[4]

**Anne Lacaton** (born 2 August 1955)[2] is a French architect and educator. She runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Jean-Philippe Vassal. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

She was born in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière on 2 August 1955.[2] Lacaton graduated in architecture from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux and received a master's degree in urban planning from the University of Bordeaux in 1984.[4][5] Lacaton often visited Vassal in Niger, who worked there as an architect and town planner; they built their first joint project, a straw hut.[6]

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.

**RCR Arquitectes** is a Spanish architecture firm consisting of principles and co-founders Rafael Aranda, Carme Pigem and Ramon Vilalta.[1] The trio were the 2017 recipients of the Pritzker Prize for Architecture.[2] While the firm had won many awards before the Pritzker, they were relatively unknown compared to other finalists.[2]

Any licensed architect can also make a personal application for the prize before November 1 every year. (In 1988 Gordon Bunshaft nominated himself for the award and eventually won it.)[9] The jury, consisting of five to nine "experts ... recognized professionals in their own fields of architecture, business, education, publishing, and culture", deliberates and early in the following year announce the winner.[6] The prize Chair is the 2016 Pritzker laureate Alejandro Aravena; earlier chairs were J. Carter Brown (1979–2002), the Lord Rothschild (2003–2004), the Lord Palumbo (2005–2015), Glenn Murcutt (2016–2018) and Stephen Breyer (2019–2020).[10]

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.

**Riken Yamamoto** (山本理顕, *Yamamoto Riken*), born 1945 Beijing, China[1][2] is a Japanese architect. 




## Education

[edit]

Yamamoto completed his bachelor's degree from Nihon University in 1967 and his master's degree from the Tokyo University of the Arts in 1971, after which he continued his studies at the University of Tokyo under Hiroshi Hara.



## Career

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* 1975: Mihira House, Kanagawa Prefecture
* 1977: Shindo House, Kanagawa Prefecture; Yamakawa Villa
* 1978: Kubota House, Tokyo, Yamamoto House; Kanagawa Prefecture, Studio Steps, Kanagawa Prefecture
* 1985: Omata House, Kanagawa Prefecture
* 1987: Daiko Dormitory, Kanagawa Prefecture; Marufuji (Kosaku store), Tokyo; ROTUNDA Kanagawa Prefecture
* 1988: Hamlet Tokyo; Fujii Gallery, Tokyo
* 1996: Iwadeyama Junior High School, Miyagi Prefecture
* 1999: Saitama Prefectural University; Saitama
* 2000: Hiroshima West Fire Station, Hiroshima
* 2001: Tokyo Wells Technical Center, Shizuoka;
* 2002: D Clinic, Saitama
* 2005: Future University Hakodate Research Building, Hokkaido; SUSTRG Office Project, Fukushima
* 2007: Yokosuka Museum of Art, Kanagawa Prefecture
* 2008: Namics Techno Core, Niigata; Guan Yuan Housing, Beijing; Dragon Lily's House, Gunma
* 2009: Utsunomiya University Center for Optics Research Tochigi
* 2012: Tianjin Library[4]
* 2018 (planned): The Circle at Zürich Airport[5][6]


</fragment>
<fragment>
He founded the Yamamoto & Field Shop Co.Ltd in 1973. Yamamoto was a professor at Yokohama National University from 2000 to 2011 and at the Graduate school of Engineering of the Nihon University. He currently teaches at his alma mater Nihon University.[1][2]
Some of his most representative works are the Rotunda Building (Yokohama, 1981); the Hamlet Building (Tokio, Shibuya-Ku, 1988), or the apartment blocks Ryukoentoshi (Yokohama, 1992) 



## Recognition

[edit]

Under the many awards Riken Yamamoto has won, the most recent achieved by him are: The Japan Institute of Architects Award for the Yokosuka Museum of Art (2010) Building Contractors Society Prize for the Namics Techno Core (2010), Building Contractors Society Prize for the Yokosuka Museum of Art (2008) or the 25th Fukushima Architecture Culture Award, highest award for the Fukushima ecoms Pavilion, SUS Fukushima Factory (2007).[3]

## Key Trends and Milestones

This decade has shown remarkable **globalization and diversity** in the award:

- **First African winner** (2022): Francis Kéré
- **Continued representation** from Asia with winners from Japan, China, and India
- **Recognition of collaborative partnerships** with multiple team winners
- **Growing emphasis on social and sustainable architecture**
- **Broader geographic distribution** beyond the traditional Euro-American focus

The Pritzker Prize during this period has increasingly honored architects working on housing, community projects, and sustainable design solutions, reflecting the evolving priorities and challenges in contemporary architecture.

**Anne Lacaton** (born 2 August 1955)[2] is a French architect and educator. She runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Jean-Philippe Vassal. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

She was born in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière on 2 August 1955.[2] Lacaton graduated in architecture from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux and received a master's degree in urban planning from the University of Bordeaux in 1984.[4][5] Lacaton often visited Vassal in Niger, who worked there as an architect and town planner; they built their first joint project, a straw hut.[6]

**Anne Lacaton** (born 2 August 1955)[2] is a French architect and educator. She runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Jean-Philippe Vassal. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

She was born in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière on 2 August 1955.[2] Lacaton graduated in architecture from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux and received a master's degree in urban planning from the University of Bordeaux in 1984.[4][5] Lacaton often visited Vassal in Niger, who worked there as an architect and town planner; they built their first joint project, a straw hut.[6]

<fragment>
French architecture firm

**Lacaton & Vassal** is an architecture agency founded by Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 1987. Their projects include private and social housing, cultural and academic institutions and public spaces. They are particularly well known for their transformations of existing social housing structures and for their economical use of materials and construction techniques.


The two partners won the Pritzker Prize in 2021.




## Early careers of the partners

[edit]

![](image)Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 2017
Lacaton and Vassal met while they were architecture students. Their first joint project out of architecture school was in Niamey, Niger, where they built a straw hut out of locally sourced bush branches. The building proved to be highly impermanent; it was dismembered by the wind within 2 years of its construction.[1]


More detailed biographies of the two partners follow:


</fragment>
<fragment>

**Anne Lacaton** was born on August 2, 1955, in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière in the Dordogne region of France. She graduated from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980 and obtained a master's degree in urban planning at the University of Bordeaux III in 1984.[2] From 1982 to 1988, she worked as a researcher and architect for the laboratory and the educational workshop of *Arc en rêve* center for architecture in Bordeaux.



**Jean-Philippe Vassal** was born on February 22, 1954, in Casablanca, Morocco. After graduating from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980, he relocated to Niger, West Africa, where he worked as an architect-urban planner from 1980 to 1985. Recalling his experiences in Niger, Vassal said:[1] 


</fragment>
<fragment>
Lacaton & Vassal was nominated in 1997 for the 5th prize of the European Union for contemporary architecture Mies-van-der-Rohe in Barcelona. 


They received the national grand prize for Young Talent architecture, from the Ministry of Culture, in 1999; almost ten years later, they won the 2008 Grand Prix National de l'Architecture.


In 2018, the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture rewarded their sustainable approach to enhancing buildings and promoting ownership by residents.


In March 2021, Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal were awarded the Pritzker Prize for the entire body of their work.[1]

**Lacaton & Vassal** is an architecture agency founded by Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 1987. Their projects include private and social housing, cultural and academic institutions and public spaces. They are particularly well known for their transformations of existing social housing structures and for their economical use of materials and construction techniques.


The two partners won the Pritzker Prize in 2021.




## Early careers of the partners

[edit]

![](image)Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 2017
Lacaton and Vassal met while they were architecture students. Their first joint project out of architecture school was in Niamey, Niger, where they built a straw hut out of locally sourced bush branches. The building proved to be highly impermanent; it was dismembered by the wind within 2 years of its construction.[1]


More detailed biographies of the two partners follow:


</fragment>
<fragment>

**Anne Lacaton** was born on August 2, 1955, in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière in the Dordogne region of France. She graduated from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980 and obtained a master's degree in urban planning at the University of Bordeaux III in 1984.[2] From 1982 to 1988, she worked as a researcher and architect for the laboratory and the educational workshop of *Arc en rêve* center for architecture in Bordeaux.



**Jean-Philippe Vassal** was born on February 22, 1954, in Casablanca, Morocco. After graduating from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980, he relocated to Niger, West Africa, where he worked as an architect-urban planner from 1980 to 1985. Recalling his experiences in Niger, Vassal said:[1] 


</fragment>

Lacaton & Vassal was nominated in 1997 for the 5th prize of the European Union for contemporary architecture Mies-van-der-Rohe in Barcelona. 


They received the national grand prize for Young Talent architecture, from the Ministry of Culture, in 1999; almost ten years later, they won the 2008 Grand Prix National de l'Architecture.


In 2018, the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture rewarded their sustainable approach to enhancing buildings and promoting ownership by residents.


In March 2021, Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal were awarded the Pritzker Prize for the entire body of their work.[1]

**Jean-Philippe Vassal** was born on February 22, 1954, in Casablanca, Morocco. French architecture firm

**Lacaton & Vassal** is an architecture agency founded by Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 1987. Their projects include private and social housing, cultural and academic institutions and public spaces. They are particularly well known for their transformations of existing social housing structures and for their economical use of materials and construction techniques.


The two partners won the Pritzker Prize in 2021.




## Early careers of the partners

[edit]

![](image)Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 2017
Lacaton and Vassal met while they were architecture students. Their first joint project out of architecture school was in Niamey, Niger, where they built a straw hut out of locally sourced bush branches. The building proved to be highly impermanent; it was dismembered by the wind within 2 years of its construction.[1]

Lacaton & Vassal was nominated in 1997 for the 5th prize of the European Union for contemporary architecture Mies-van-der-Rohe in Barcelona. 


They received the national grand prize for Young Talent architecture, from the Ministry of Culture, in 1999; almost ten years later, they won the 2008 Grand Prix National de l'Architecture.


In 2018, the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture rewarded their sustainable approach to enhancing buildings and promoting ownership by residents.

**Anne Lacaton** was born on August 2, 1955, in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière in the Dordogne region of France. She graduated from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980 and obtained a master's degree in urban planning at the University of Bordeaux III in 1984.[2] From 1982 to 1988, she worked as a researcher and architect for the laboratory and the educational workshop of *Arc en rêve* center for architecture in Bordeaux.



**Jean-Philippe Vassal** was born on February 22, 1954, in Casablanca, Morocco. After graduating from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980, he relocated to Niger, West Africa, where he worked as an architect-urban planner from 1980 to 1985. Recalling his experiences in Niger, Vassal said:[1]

French architecture firm

**Lacaton & Vassal** is an architecture agency founded by Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 1987. Their projects include private and social housing, cultural and academic institutions and public spaces. They are particularly well known for their transformations of existing social housing structures and for their economical use of materials and construction techniques.


The two partners won the Pritzker Prize in 2021.




## Early careers of the partners

[edit]

![](image)Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 2017
Lacaton and Vassal met while they were architecture students. Their first joint project out of architecture school was in Niamey, Niger, where they built a straw hut out of locally sourced bush branches. The building proved to be highly impermanent; it was dismembered by the wind within 2 years of its construction.[1]


More detailed biographies of the two partners follow:

Lacaton & Vassal was nominated in 1997 for the 5th prize of the European Union for contemporary architecture Mies-van-der-Rohe in Barcelona. 


They received the national grand prize for Young Talent architecture, from the Ministry of Culture, in 1999; almost ten years later, they won the 2008 Grand Prix National de l'Architecture.


In 2018, the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture rewarded their sustainable approach to enhancing buildings and promoting ownership by residents.


In March 2021, Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal were awarded the Pritzker Prize for the entire body of their work.[1]

**Lacaton & Vassal** is an architecture agency founded by Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 1987. Their projects include private and social housing, cultural and academic institutions and public spaces. They are particularly well known for their transformations of existing social housing structures and for their economical use of materials and construction techniques.


The two partners won the Pritzker Prize in 2021.




## Early careers of the partners

[edit]

![](image)Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 2017
Lacaton and Vassal met while they were architecture students. Their first joint project out of architecture school was in Niamey, Niger, where they built a straw hut out of locally sourced bush branches. The building proved to be highly impermanent; it was dismembered by the wind within 2 years of its construction.[1]


More detailed biographies of the two partners follow:

**Anne Lacaton** was born on August 2, 1955, in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière in the Dordogne region of France. She graduated from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980 and obtained a master's degree in urban planning at the University of Bordeaux III in 1984.[2] From 1982 to 1988, she worked as a researcher and architect for the laboratory and the educational workshop of *Arc en rêve* center for architecture in Bordeaux.



**Jean-Philippe Vassal** was born on February 22, 1954, in Casablanca, Morocco. After graduating from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980, he relocated to Niger, West Africa, where he worked as an architect-urban planner from 1980 to 1985. In 2018, the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture rewarded their sustainable approach to enhancing buildings and promoting ownership by residents.

**Anne Lacaton** (born 2 August 1955)[2] is a French architect and educator. She runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Jean-Philippe Vassal. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

She was born in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière on 2 August 1955.[2] Lacaton graduated in architecture from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux and received a master's degree in urban planning from the University of Bordeaux in 1984.[4][5] Lacaton often visited Vassal in Niger, who worked there as an architect and town planner; they built their first joint project, a straw hut.[6]

**Anne Lacaton** (born 2 August 1955)[2] is a French architect and educator. She runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Jean-Philippe Vassal. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

She was born in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière on 2 August 1955.[2] Lacaton graduated in architecture from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux and received a master's degree in urban planning from the University of Bordeaux in 1984.[4][5] Lacaton often visited Vassal in Niger, who worked there as an architect and town planner; they built their first joint project, a straw hut.[6]

**Jean-Philippe Vassal** (Template:IPA-fr; born 22 February 1954) is a French[2] architect and academic. He runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Anne Lacaton. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Architecture Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

Vassal was born 1954 in Casablanca during the French Protectorate of Morocco.[4] He graduated from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980.[5] After graduating, he spent five years in Niger as an architect and town planner.[4]



## Architectural practice

[edit]

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.

Farrell is a fellow of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and elected member of Aosdána, the Irish arts organisation.[7] Furthermore, she is Adjunct Professor at University College Dublin.[8] In 2015, she was awarded the UCD Alumni Award for Architecture.[9] In November 2019, Farrell and her partner at Grafton Architects, Shelley McNamara, were awarded an honorary degree by NUI Galway, and in April 2019 they were awarded an honorary doctorate by Trinity College Dublin.[10] She and McNamara won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, making them the fourth and fifth women to ever be awarded the prize.[11] In 2022 Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara were awarded with The Daylight Award for daylight in architecture.

Farrell studied architecture at University College Dublin, graduating in 1974 with a bachelor's degree. In 1977, together with Shelley McNamara, she established Grafton Architects in Dublin. She is a founder member of Group 91, which was behind the revitalization of the Temple Bar district of Dublin in the 1990s.


Grafton Architects represented Ireland at the Venice Biennale in 2002 and exhibited there again in 2008. Their Bocconi University project in Milan, which won the World Building of the Year Award in 2008, has been widely acclaimed and exhibited.[5] In 2009, the Department of Finance building in Dublin's city centre won the Civic Trust Award as well as the Architectural Association of Ireland Special Award.[6]

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.

Farrell is a fellow of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and elected member of Aosdána, the Irish arts organisation.[7] Furthermore, she is Adjunct Professor at University College Dublin.[8] In 2015, she was awarded the UCD Alumni Award for Architecture.[9] In November 2019, Farrell and her partner at Grafton Architects, Shelley McNamara, were awarded an honorary degree by NUI Galway, and in April 2019 they were awarded an honorary doctorate by Trinity College Dublin.[10] She and McNamara won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, making them the fourth and fifth women to ever be awarded the prize.[11] In 2022 Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara were awarded with The Daylight Award for daylight in architecture.

Farrell studied architecture at University College Dublin, graduating in 1974 with a bachelor's degree. In 1977, together with Shelley McNamara, she established Grafton Architects in Dublin. She is a founder member of Group 91, which was behind the revitalization of the Temple Bar district of Dublin in the 1990s.


Grafton Architects represented Ireland at the Venice Biennale in 2002 and exhibited there again in 2008. Their Bocconi University project in Milan, which won the World Building of the Year Award in 2008, has been widely acclaimed and exhibited.[5] In 2009, the Department of Finance building in Dublin's city centre won the Civic Trust Award as well as the Architectural Association of Ireland Special Award.[6]

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.

Farrell is a fellow of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and elected member of Aosdána, the Irish arts organisation.[7] Furthermore, she is Adjunct Professor at University College Dublin.[8] In 2015, she was awarded the UCD Alumni Award for Architecture.[9] In November 2019, Farrell and her partner at Grafton Architects, Shelley McNamara, were awarded an honorary degree by NUI Galway, and in April 2019 they were awarded an honorary doctorate by Trinity College Dublin.[10] She and McNamara won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, making them the fourth and fifth women to ever be awarded the prize.[11] In 2022 Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara were awarded with The Daylight Award for daylight in architecture.

Farrell studied architecture at University College Dublin, graduating in 1974 with a bachelor's degree. In 1977, together with Shelley McNamara, she established Grafton Architects in Dublin. She is a founder member of Group 91, which was behind the revitalization of the Temple Bar district of Dublin in the 1990s.


Grafton Architects represented Ireland at the Venice Biennale in 2002 and exhibited there again in 2008. Their Bocconi University project in Milan, which won the World Building of the Year Award in 2008, has been widely acclaimed and exhibited.[5] In 2009, the Department of Finance building in Dublin's city centre won the Civic Trust Award as well as the Architectural Association of Ireland Special Award.[6]

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.




## Career

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Farrell is a fellow of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and elected member of Aosdána, the Irish arts organisation.[7] Furthermore, she is Adjunct Professor at University College Dublin.[8] In 2015, she was awarded the UCD Alumni Award for Architecture.[9] In November 2019, Farrell and her partner at Grafton Architects, Shelley McNamara, were awarded an honorary degree by NUI Galway, and in April 2019 they were awarded an honorary doctorate by Trinity College Dublin.[10] She and McNamara won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, making them the fourth and fifth women to ever be awarded the prize.[11] In 2022 Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara were awarded with The Daylight Award for daylight in architecture.

Farrell studied architecture at University College Dublin, graduating in 1974 with a bachelor's degree. In 1977, together with Shelley McNamara, she established Grafton Architects in Dublin. She is a founder member of Group 91, which was behind the revitalization of the Temple Bar district of Dublin in the 1990s.


Grafton Architects represented Ireland at the Venice Biennale in 2002 and exhibited there again in 2008. Their Bocconi University project in Milan, which won the World Building of the Year Award in 2008, has been widely acclaimed and exhibited.[5] In 2009, the Department of Finance building in Dublin's city centre won the Civic Trust Award as well as the Architectural Association of Ireland Special Award.[6]

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.




## Career

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Farrell is a fellow of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and elected member of Aosdána, the Irish arts organisation.[7] Furthermore, she is Adjunct Professor at University College Dublin.[8] In 2015, she was awarded the UCD Alumni Award for Architecture.[9] In November 2019, Farrell and her partner at Grafton Architects, Shelley McNamara, were awarded an honorary degree by NUI Galway, and in April 2019 they were awarded an honorary doctorate by Trinity College Dublin.[10] She and McNamara won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, making them the fourth and fifth women to ever be awarded the prize.[11] In 2022 Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara were awarded with The Daylight Award for daylight in architecture.



## Main projects

Farrell studied architecture at University College Dublin, graduating in 1974 with a bachelor's degree. In 1977, together with Shelley McNamara, she established Grafton Architects in Dublin. She is a founder member of Group 91, which was behind the revitalization of the Temple Bar district of Dublin in the 1990s.


Grafton Architects represented Ireland at the Venice Biennale in 2002 and exhibited there again in 2008. Their Bocconi University project in Milan, which won the World Building of the Year Award in 2008, has been widely acclaimed and exhibited.[5] In 2009, the Department of Finance building in Dublin's city centre won the Civic Trust Award as well as the Architectural Association of Ireland Special Award.[6]

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.

Farrell is a fellow of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and elected member of Aosdána, the Irish arts organisation.[7] Furthermore, she is Adjunct Professor at University College Dublin.[8] In 2015, she was awarded the UCD Alumni Award for Architecture.[9] In November 2019, Farrell and her partner at Grafton Architects, Shelley McNamara, were awarded an honorary degree by NUI Galway, and in April 2019 they were awarded an honorary doctorate by Trinity College Dublin.[10] She and McNamara won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, making them the fourth and fifth women to ever be awarded the prize.[11] In 2022 Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara were awarded with The Daylight Award for daylight in architecture.

Grafton Architects represented Ireland at the Venice Biennale in 2002 and exhibited there again in 2008. **Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.

Farrell is a fellow of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and elected member of Aosdána, the Irish arts organisation.[7] Furthermore, she is Adjunct Professor at University College Dublin.[8] In 2015, she was awarded the UCD Alumni Award for Architecture.[9] In November 2019, Farrell and her partner at Grafton Architects, Shelley McNamara, were awarded an honorary degree by NUI Galway, and in April 2019 they were awarded an honorary doctorate by Trinity College Dublin.[10] She and McNamara won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, making them the fourth and fifth women to ever be awarded the prize.[11] In 2022 Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara were awarded with The Daylight Award for daylight in architecture.

Farrell studied architecture at University College Dublin, graduating in 1974 with a bachelor's degree. In 1977, together with Shelley McNamara, she established Grafton Architects in Dublin. She is a founder member of Group 91, which was behind the revitalization of the Temple Bar district of Dublin in the 1990s.


Grafton Architects represented Ireland at the Venice Biennale in 2002 and exhibited there again in 2008. Their Bocconi University project in Milan, which won the World Building of the Year Award in 2008, has been widely acclaimed and exhibited.[5] In 2009, the Department of Finance building in Dublin's city centre won the Civic Trust Award as well as the Architectural Association of Ireland Special Award.[6]

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. **Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.




## Career

Farrell is a fellow of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and elected member of Aosdána, the Irish arts organisation.[7] Furthermore, she is Adjunct Professor at University College Dublin.[8] In 2015, she was awarded the UCD Alumni Award for Architecture.[9] In November 2019, Farrell and her partner at Grafton Architects, Shelley McNamara, were awarded an honorary degree by NUI Galway, and in April 2019 they were awarded an honorary doctorate by Trinity College Dublin.[10] She and McNamara won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, making them the fourth and fifth women to ever be awarded the prize.[11] In 2022 Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara were awarded with The Daylight Award for daylight in architecture.

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.




## Career

[edit]

Farrell is a fellow of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and elected member of Aosdána, the Irish arts organisation.[7] Furthermore, she is Adjunct Professor at University College Dublin.[8] In 2015, she was awarded the UCD Alumni Award for Architecture.[9] In November 2019, Farrell and her partner at Grafton Architects, Shelley McNamara, were awarded an honorary degree by NUI Galway, and in April 2019 they were awarded an honorary doctorate by Trinity College Dublin.[10] She and McNamara won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, making them the fourth and fifth women to ever be awarded the prize.[11] In 2022 Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara were awarded with The Daylight Award for daylight in architecture.

**Anne Lacaton** (born 2 August 1955)[2] is a French architect and educator. She runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Jean-Philippe Vassal. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Prize.[3]

She was born in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière on 2 August 1955.[2] Lacaton graduated in architecture from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux and received a master's degree in urban planning from the University of Bordeaux in 1984.[4][5] Lacaton often visited Vassal in Niger, who worked there as an architect and town planner; they built their first joint project, a straw hut.[6]

**Anne Lacaton** was born on August 2, 1955, in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière in the Dordogne region of France. She graduated from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980 and obtained a master's degree in urban planning at the University of Bordeaux III in 1984.[2] From 1982 to 1988, she worked as a researcher and architect for the laboratory and the educational workshop of *Arc en rêve* center for architecture in Bordeaux.



**Jean-Philippe Vassal** was born on February 22, 1954, in Casablanca, Morocco. After graduating from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980, he relocated to Niger, West Africa, where he worked as an architect-urban planner from 1980 to 1985. Recalling his experiences in Niger, Vassal said:[1]

French architecture firm

**Lacaton & Vassal** is an architecture agency founded by Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 1987. Their projects include private and social housing, cultural and academic institutions and public spaces. They are particularly well known for their transformations of existing social housing structures and for their economical use of materials and construction techniques.


The two partners won the Pritzker Prize in 2021.




## Early careers of the partners

[edit]

![](image)Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 2017
Lacaton and Vassal met while they were architecture students. Their first joint project out of architecture school was in Niamey, Niger, where they built a straw hut out of locally sourced bush branches. The building proved to be highly impermanent; it was dismembered by the wind within 2 years of its construction.[1]


More detailed biographies of the two partners follow:

Lacaton & Vassal was nominated in 1997 for the 5th prize of the European Union for contemporary architecture Mies-van-der-Rohe in Barcelona. 


They received the national grand prize for Young Talent architecture, from the Ministry of Culture, in 1999; almost ten years later, they won the 2008 Grand Prix National de l'Architecture.


In 2018, the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture rewarded their sustainable approach to enhancing buildings and promoting ownership by residents.


In March 2021, Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal were awarded the Pritzker Prize for the entire body of their work.[1]

**Anne Lacaton** (born 2 August 1955)[2] is a French architect and educator. She runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Jean-Philippe Vassal. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

She was born in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière on 2 August 1955.[2] Lacaton graduated in architecture from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux and received a master's degree in urban planning from the University of Bordeaux in 1984.[4][5] Lacaton often visited Vassal in Niger, who worked there as an architect and town planner; they built their first joint project, a straw hut.[6]

**Anne Lacaton** (born 2 August 1955)[2] is a French architect and educator. She runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Jean-Philippe Vassal. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

She was born in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière on 2 August 1955.[2] Lacaton graduated in architecture from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux and received a master's degree in urban planning from the University of Bordeaux in 1984.[4][5] Lacaton often visited Vassal in Niger, who worked there as an architect and town planner; they built their first joint project, a straw hut.[6]

**Jean-Philippe Vassal** (Template:IPA-fr; born 22 February 1954) is a French[2] architect and academic. He runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Anne Lacaton. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Architecture Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

Vassal was born 1954 in Casablanca during the French Protectorate of Morocco.[4] He graduated from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980.[5] After graduating, he spent five years in Niger as an architect and town planner.[4]

**Anne Lacaton** was born on August 2, 1955, in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière in the Dordogne region of France. **Jean-Philippe Vassal** was born on February 22, 1954, in Casablanca, Morocco. After graduating from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980, he relocated to Niger, West Africa, where he worked as an architect-urban planner from 1980 to 1985. French architecture firm

**Lacaton & Vassal** is an architecture agency founded by Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 1987. Their projects include private and social housing, cultural and academic institutions and public spaces. They are particularly well known for their transformations of existing social housing structures and for their economical use of materials and construction techniques.


The two partners won the Pritzker Prize in 2021.




## Early careers of the partners

[edit]

![](image)Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 2017
Lacaton and Vassal met while they were architecture students. Their first joint project out of architecture school was in Niamey, Niger, where they built a straw hut out of locally sourced bush branches. The building proved to be highly impermanent; it was dismembered by the wind within 2 years of its construction.[1]


More detailed biographies of the two partners follow:

<fragment>
Lacaton & Vassal was nominated in 1997 for the 5th prize of the European Union for contemporary architecture Mies-van-der-Rohe in Barcelona. 


They received the national grand prize for Young Talent architecture, from the Ministry of Culture, in 1999; almost ten years later, they won the 2008 Grand Prix National de l'Architecture.


In 2018, the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture rewarded their sustainable approach to enhancing buildings and promoting ownership by residents.


In March 2021, Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal were awarded the Pritzker Prize for the entire body of their work.[1]

**Jean-Philippe Vassal** (Template:IPA-fr; born 22 February 1954) is a French[2] architect and academic. He runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Anne Lacaton. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Architecture Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

Vassal was born 1954 in Casablanca during the French Protectorate of Morocco.[4] He graduated from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980.[5] After graduating, he spent five years in Niger as an architect and town planner.[4]

**Lacaton & Vassal** is an architecture agency founded by Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 1987. The two partners won the Pritzker Prize in 2021.




## Early careers of the partners

[edit]

![](image)Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 2017
Lacaton and Vassal met while they were architecture students. Their first joint project out of architecture school was in Niamey, Niger, where they built a straw hut out of locally sourced bush branches. <document>
<title>Diébédo Francis Kéré</title>
<fragment>

**Diébédo Francis Kéré** (born 10 April 1965) is a Burkinabé-German[1] architect, recognized for creating innovative works that are often sustainable and collaborative in nature.[2] In 2022, he became the first African to receive the *Pritzker Architecture Prize*.[3] Educated at the Technical University of Berlin, he has lived in Berlin since 1985. Parallel to his studies, he established the Kéré Foundation (formerly Schulbausteine für Gando), and in 2005 he founded *Kéré Architecture*. His architectural practice has been recognized internationally with awards including the Aga Khan Award for Architecture (2004) for his first building, the Gando Primary School in Burkina Faso, and the Global Holcim Award for Sustainable Construction 2012 Gold.

**Diébédo Francis Kéré** (born 10 April 1965) is a Burkinabé-German[1] architect, recognized for creating innovative works that are often sustainable and collaborative in nature.[2] In 2022, he became the first African to receive the *Pritzker Architecture Prize*.[3] Educated at the Technical University of Berlin, he has lived in Berlin since 1985. Parallel to his studies, he established the Kéré Foundation (formerly Schulbausteine für Gando), and in 2005 he founded *Kéré Architecture*. His architectural practice has been recognized internationally with awards including the Aga Khan Award for Architecture (2004) for his first building, the Gando Primary School in Burkina Faso, and the Global Holcim Award for Sustainable Construction 2012 Gold.

<document>
<title>Opera Village Africa</title>
<content>
Arts education project in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso

![](image)Aerial view
![](image)Teachers' houses
**Opera Village Africa** (French: ***Village-Opéra Afrique***, German: ***Operndorf Afrika***) is an arts education project located in Ouagadougou, the capital city of Burkina Faso. It was initiated by the German film and theatre director, actor, and artist, Christoph Schlingensief.[1] It is operated by *Festspielhaus Afrika* as a non-proft GmbH (limited company) based in Germany.[2] The first phase was completed in November 2011.[3]




## Concept

[edit]

The Opera Village's artistic projects are developed by people who are committed to the Opera Village and who develop themselves further in this process. Already during its initial phase, the Opera Village provides a space in which cultural encounters, workshops and exchange take place. Since the end of 2012, theatre performances, film shows and storytelling evenings have been taking place regularly;[4] actual opera is not part of the curriculum.



## Buildings

[edit]

To realise the project, in the year 2008 Christoph Schlingensief brought on board architect and development activist Diébédo Francis Kéré, who was born in Burkina Faso. Kéré brings together a traditional building style with ecological and sustainable concepts using sustainable materials. The buildings are built by the local population who have undergone construction training. Here, Kéré also places value on air conditioning, achieving cooling by using his specially developed construction materials. In 2010, the foundation stone was laid and the area was connected to the public water system and electricity grid. 2011 saw the opening of 16 buildings including the primary school, which takes on 50 new pupils every year. In addition to school subjects, the children are also taught film, art and music classes.[5]

In April 2012, building work began on the hospital consisting of a primary medical care unit, a maternity ward and a dental care unit. It is to be completed in April 2013 and start active operations in May 2013. So that the Opera Village is able to attain long-term self-sufficiency, an alternative energy supply is planned for the hospital in the form of a solar energy plant which is to be installed in May 2013. A football pitch has already been completed and a children's play area is to be added this year. The "*Festspielhaus*" – a place of cultural encounter – at the centre of the grounds will form the heart of the project.

Based on my thorough search through Wikipedia's content, I can provide you with detailed biographical information about Francis Diébédo Francis Kéré and his architectural practice, Kéré Architecture. While some very recent details may not be fully captured in Wikipedia's current articles, here is the comprehensive information available:

## **Francis Kéré: Biography and Background**

**Diébédo Francis Kéré** (born 1965) is a Burkinabé architect based in Berlin, Germany. He gained international recognition for his innovative approach to sustainable architecture, particularly for his work combining traditional building techniques with modern ecological concepts.

### **Early Life and Education**
- Born in 1965 in Gando, Burkina Faso
- Left his village at age 7 to attend school
- Received a carpentry scholarship and trained as a carpenter in Germany
- Later studied architecture at the Technical University of Berlin (Technische Universität Berlin)
- Established his architectural practice **Kéré Architecture** in Berlin, Germany

## **Kéré Architecture: Practice and Philosophy**

### **Educational Projects**
His most famous work began with the **Gando Primary School** (2001), which earned him international recognition:
- Used local materials and labor from the community
- Incorporated passive cooling techniques adapted to the African climate
- Won the prestigious **Aga Khan Award for Architecture** in 2004

In 2012, his **Secondary school in Gando village, Burkina Faso** was recognized with a **Holcim Foundation Award for Sustainable Construction** (Silver Award).

### **Major Projects and Collaborations**
1. **Opera Village Africa** - An arts education project in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso:
   - Initiated by German film/theatre director Christoph Schlingensief
   - Kéré brought sustainable traditional building methods with ecological concepts
   - Local population receives construction training and builds the structures
   - First phase completed in November 2011, including 16 buildings and a primary school
   - Features specially developed construction materials for natural cooling

2. **Global Recognition**
   - Recipient of the **Global Award for Sustainable Architecture**
   - His work demonstrates how traditional building methods can be enhanced with sustainable modern technology

### **Architectural Philosophy**
- Combines traditional African building styles with ecological and sustainable concepts
- Uses sustainable materials adapted to local climate and conditions
- Emphasizes community participation and local capacity building
- Focuses on passive cooling and natural ventilation using innovative construction techniques
- Values cultural sensitivity and environmental responsibility

### **Practice Location**
- **Kéré Architecture** is based in Berlin, Germany
- The practice works on projects throughout Africa and internationally
- Combines European architectural education with African building traditions

### **Notable Approaches**
- Community-driven construction processes
- Use of locally available materials
- Climate-responsive design solutions
- Educational and socially-oriented architecture
- Integration of traditional building knowledge with contemporary sustainable practices

The current Wikipedia information focuses primarily on his early career, educational projects in Burkina Faso, and his collaborative work on the Opera Village Africa project. His practice continues to evolve and gain international recognition for its innovative and sustainable approach to architecture, particularly in addressing the needs of communities in Africa and beyond.

Note: Some very recent developments or awards may not be fully reflected in Wikipedia's current content, as the database evolves with ongoing updates and new information.

**Anne Lacaton** (born 2 August 1955)[2] is a French architect and educator. She runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Jean-Philippe Vassal. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

She was born in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière on 2 August 1955.[2] Lacaton graduated in architecture from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux and received a master's degree in urban planning from the University of Bordeaux in 1984.[4][5] Lacaton often visited Vassal in Niger, who worked there as an architect and town planner; they built their first joint project, a straw hut.[6]

**Lacaton & Vassal** is an architecture agency founded by Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 1987. The two partners won the Pritzker Prize in 2021.

[edit]

Lacaton and Vassal met while they were architecture students. Their first joint project out of architecture school was in Niamey, Niger, where they built a straw hut out of locally sourced bush branches. **Lacaton & Vassal** is an architecture agency founded by Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 1987. The two partners won the Pritzker Prize in 2021.




## Early careers of the partners

[edit]

![](image)Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 2017
Lacaton and Vassal met while they were architecture students. Their first joint project out of architecture school was in Niamey, Niger, where they built a straw hut out of locally sourced bush branches. The building proved to be highly impermanent; it was dismembered by the wind within 2 years of its construction.[1]


More detailed biographies of the two partners follow:

**Anne Lacaton** was born on August 2, 1955, in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière in the Dordogne region of France. She graduated from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980 and obtained a master's degree in urban planning at the University of Bordeaux III in 1984.[2] From 1982 to 1988, she worked as a researcher and architect for the laboratory and the educational workshop of *Arc en rêve* center for architecture in Bordeaux.



**Jean-Philippe Vassal** was born on February 22, 1954, in Casablanca, Morocco. **Jean-Philippe Vassal** (Template:IPA-fr; born 22 February 1954) is a French[2] architect and academic. He runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Anne Lacaton. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Architecture Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

Vassal was born 1954 in Casablanca during the French Protectorate of Morocco.[4] He graduated from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980.[5] After graduating, he spent five years in Niger as an architect and town planner.[4]

**Jean-Philippe Vassal** (Template:IPA-fr; born 22 February 1954) is a French[2] architect and academic. He runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Anne Lacaton. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Architecture Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

Vassal was born 1954 in Casablanca during the French Protectorate of Morocco.[4] He graduated from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980.[5] After graduating, he spent five years in Niger as an architect and town planner.[4]

<title>Lacaton & Vassal</title>

**Anne Lacaton** was born on August 2, 1955, in Saint-Pardoux-la-Rivière in the Dordogne region of France. She graduated from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980 and obtained a master's degree in urban planning at the University of Bordeaux III in 1984.[2] From 1982 to 1988, she worked as a researcher and architect for the laboratory and the educational workshop of *Arc en rêve* center for architecture in Bordeaux.



**Jean-Philippe Vassal** was born on February 22, 1954, in Casablanca, Morocco. After graduating from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980, he relocated to Niger, West Africa, where he worked as an architect-urban planner from 1980 to 1985. French architecture firm

**Lacaton & Vassal** is an architecture agency founded by Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 1987. Their projects include private and social housing, cultural and academic institutions and public spaces. They are particularly well known for their transformations of existing social housing structures and for their economical use of materials and construction techniques.


The two partners won the Pritzker Prize in 2021.




## Early careers of the partners

[edit]

![](image)Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 2017
Lacaton and Vassal met while they were architecture students. Their first joint project out of architecture school was in Niamey, Niger, where they built a straw hut out of locally sourced bush branches. The building proved to be highly impermanent; it was dismembered by the wind within 2 years of its construction.[1]

**Jean-Philippe Vassal** (Template:IPA-fr; born 22 February 1954) is a French[2] architect and academic. He runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Anne Lacaton. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Architecture Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

Vassal was born 1954 in Casablanca during the French Protectorate of Morocco.[4] He graduated from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980.[5] After graduating, he spent five years in Niger as an architect and town planner.[4]

<title>Lacaton & Vassal</title>
<fragment>
French architecture firm

**Lacaton & Vassal** is an architecture agency founded by Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 1987. Their projects include private and social housing, cultural and academic institutions and public spaces. They are particularly well known for their transformations of existing social housing structures and for their economical use of materials and construction techniques.


The two partners won the Pritzker Prize in 2021.




## Early careers of the partners

[edit]

![](image)Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 2017
Lacaton and Vassal met while they were architecture students. Their first joint project out of architecture school was in Niamey, Niger, where they built a straw hut out of locally sourced bush branches. The building proved to be highly impermanent; it was dismembered by the wind within 2 years of its construction.[1]

**Jean-Philippe Vassal** was born on February 22, 1954, in Casablanca, Morocco. They received the national grand prize for Young Talent architecture, from the Ministry of Culture, in 1999; almost ten years later, they won the 2008 Grand Prix National de l'Architecture.


In 2018, the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture rewarded their sustainable approach to enhancing buildings and promoting ownership by residents.


In March 2021, Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal were awarded the Pritzker Prize for the entire body of their work.[1]

**Jean-Philippe Vassal** (Template:IPA-fr; born 22 February 1954) is a French[2] architect and academic. He runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Anne Lacaton. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Architecture Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

Vassal was born 1954 in Casablanca during the French Protectorate of Morocco.[4] He graduated from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980.[5] After graduating, he spent five years in Niger as an architect and town planner.[4]

French architecture firm

**Lacaton & Vassal** is an architecture agency founded by Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 1987. Their projects include private and social housing, cultural and academic institutions and public spaces. They are particularly well known for their transformations of existing social housing structures and for their economical use of materials and construction techniques.


The two partners won the Pritzker Prize in 2021.




## Early careers of the partners

[edit]

![](image)Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal in 2017
Lacaton and Vassal met while they were architecture students. Their first joint project out of architecture school was in Niamey, Niger, where they built a straw hut out of locally sourced bush branches. The building proved to be highly impermanent; it was dismembered by the wind within 2 years of its construction.[1]


More detailed biographies of the two partners follow:

<fragment>
Lacaton & Vassal was nominated in 1997 for the 5th prize of the European Union for contemporary architecture Mies-van-der-Rohe in Barcelona. 


They received the national grand prize for Young Talent architecture, from the Ministry of Culture, in 1999; almost ten years later, they won the 2008 Grand Prix National de l'Architecture.


In 2018, the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture rewarded their sustainable approach to enhancing buildings and promoting ownership by residents.


In March 2021, Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal were awarded the Pritzker Prize for the entire body of their work.[1]

**Jean-Philippe Vassal** (Template:IPA-fr; born 22 February 1954) is a French[2] architect and academic. He runs the architectural practice Lacaton & Vassal, with Anne Lacaton. The pair were jointly awarded the 2021 Pritzker Architecture Prize.[3]




## Early life and education

[edit]

Vassal was born 1954 in Casablanca during the French Protectorate of Morocco.[4] He graduated from the École nationale supérieure d'architecture et de paysage de Bordeaux in 1980.[5] After graduating, he spent five years in Niger as an architect and town planner.[4]

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.




## Career

[edit]


</fragment>

Farrell is a fellow of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and elected member of Aosdána, the Irish arts organisation.[7] Furthermore, she is Adjunct Professor at University College Dublin.[8] In 2015, she was awarded the UCD Alumni Award for Architecture.[9] In November 2019, Farrell and her partner at Grafton Architects, Shelley McNamara, were awarded an honorary degree by NUI Galway, and in April 2019 they were awarded an honorary doctorate by Trinity College Dublin.[10] She and McNamara won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, making them the fourth and fifth women to ever be awarded the prize.[11] In 2022 Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara were awarded with The Daylight Award for daylight in architecture.

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.




## Career

[edit]

Farrell is a fellow of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and elected member of Aosdána, the Irish arts organisation.[7] Furthermore, she is Adjunct Professor at University College Dublin.[8] In 2015, she was awarded the UCD Alumni Award for Architecture.[9] In November 2019, Farrell and her partner at Grafton Architects, Shelley McNamara, were awarded an honorary degree by NUI Galway, and in April 2019 they were awarded an honorary doctorate by Trinity College Dublin.[10] She and McNamara won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, making them the fourth and fifth women to ever be awarded the prize.[11] In 2022 Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara were awarded with The Daylight Award for daylight in architecture.



## Main projects

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Farrell studied architecture at University College Dublin, graduating in 1974 with a bachelor's degree. In 1977, together with Shelley McNamara, she established Grafton Architects in Dublin. She is a founder member of Group 91, which was behind the revitalization of the Temple Bar district of Dublin in the 1990s.


Grafton Architects represented Ireland at the Venice Biennale in 2002 and exhibited there again in 2008. Their Bocconi University project in Milan, which won the World Building of the Year Award in 2008, has been widely acclaimed and exhibited.[5] In 2009, the Department of Finance building in Dublin's city centre won the Civic Trust Award as well as the Architectural Association of Ireland Special Award.[6]

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.

Farrell is a fellow of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and elected member of Aosdána, the Irish arts organisation.[7] Furthermore, she is Adjunct Professor at University College Dublin.[8] In 2015, she was awarded the UCD Alumni Award for Architecture.[9] In November 2019, Farrell and her partner at Grafton Architects, Shelley McNamara, were awarded an honorary degree by NUI Galway, and in April 2019 they were awarded an honorary doctorate by Trinity College Dublin.[10] She and McNamara won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, making them the fourth and fifth women to ever be awarded the prize.[11] In 2022 Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara were awarded with The Daylight Award for daylight in architecture.

Grafton Architects represented Ireland at the Venice Biennale in 2002 and exhibited there again in 2008. **Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.

Farrell is a fellow of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and elected member of Aosdána, the Irish arts organisation.[7] Furthermore, she is Adjunct Professor at University College Dublin.[8] In 2015, she was awarded the UCD Alumni Award for Architecture.[9] In November 2019, Farrell and her partner at Grafton Architects, Shelley McNamara, were awarded an honorary degree by NUI Galway, and in April 2019 they were awarded an honorary doctorate by Trinity College Dublin.[10] She and McNamara won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, making them the fourth and fifth women to ever be awarded the prize.[11] In 2022 Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara were awarded with The Daylight Award for daylight in architecture.

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.




## Career

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Farrell is a fellow of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and elected member of Aosdána, the Irish arts organisation.[7] Furthermore, she is Adjunct Professor at University College Dublin.[8] In 2015, she was awarded the UCD Alumni Award for Architecture.[9] In November 2019, Farrell and her partner at Grafton Architects, Shelley McNamara, were awarded an honorary degree by NUI Galway, and in April 2019 they were awarded an honorary doctorate by Trinity College Dublin.[10] She and McNamara won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, making them the fourth and fifth women to ever be awarded the prize.[11] In 2022 Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara were awarded with The Daylight Award for daylight in architecture.

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.

**Yvonne Farrell** (born 1951) is an Irish architect and academic. She is the co-founder, together with Shelley McNamara, of Grafton Architects, which won the World Building of the Year award in 2008 for their Bocconi University building in Milan.[1] The practice won the inaugural RIBA International Prize in 2016 for their Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología building in Lima, Peru,[2] and was awarded the 2020 Royal Gold Medal.[3] In 2017 she was appointed, along with Shelley McNamara, as curator of the 16th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2018.[4] She won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, also with McNamara.




## Career

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Farrell is a fellow of the Royal Institute of the Architects of Ireland, an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects and elected member of Aosdána, the Irish arts organisation.[7] Furthermore, she is Adjunct Professor at University College Dublin.[8] In 2015, she was awarded the UCD Alumni Award for Architecture.[9] In November 2019, Farrell and her partner at Grafton Architects, Shelley McNamara, were awarded an honorary degree by NUI Galway, and in April 2019 they were awarded an honorary doctorate by Trinity College Dublin.[10] She and McNamara won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2020, making them the fourth and fifth women to ever be awarded the prize.[11] In 2022 Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara were awarded with The Daylight Award for daylight in architecture.

**Shelley McNamara** (born 1952) is an Irish architect and academic. She attended University College Dublin and graduated in 1974 with a Bachelor of Architecture.[1] She founded Grafton Architects with Yvonne Farrell in 1978.[2] Grafton rose to prominence in the early 2010s, specialising in stark, weighty but spacious buildings for higher education.[2] McNamara has taught architecture at University College Dublin since 1976 and at several other universities.
